extracted.intended_audience: environmental lawyers, regulatory advocates, agency reviewers, and federal courts evaluating EPA rulemaking and petitions for reconsideration
extracted.subtask_description: A legal petition under CAA §307(d)(7)(B) challenging EPA’s Final Rule rescinding the GHG Endangerment Finding and vehicle GHG standards, focusing on technical modeling choices, novel analyses, legal errors, and procedural notice-and-comment defects. The document identifies legal and technical criteria by which the rule is arbitrary, capricious, or procedurally invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metrics for futility/health-and-welfare evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s futility analysis relied solely on global average temperature and sea level rise as the exclusive metrics for evaluating futility, even though those intermediate metrics “are not themselves the adverse impacts on health and welfare relevant for purposes of the analysis” and “do not translate directly to adverse health and welfare impacts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must not rely exclusively on intermediate physical-climate metrics as proxies for health and welfare harms; they should instead consider direct measures of damages to society and health/welfare (e.g., extreme weather, ocean acidification, crop nutritional effects) consistent with longstanding EPA practice and commenters’ recommendations. Using only intermediate proxies without explaining their sufficiency is arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of non-CO2 greenhouse gases in modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA arbitrarily counted only vehicle CO2 emissions to the exclusion of non-CO2 greenhouse gas emissions (N2O, CH4, HFCs) for its futility analysis, despite motor vehicles unquestionably emitting such gases and EPA modeling them elsewhere in the RIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling for purposes of determining futility must include all relevant GHGs emitted by the source category when those gases contribute to climate impacts and when EPA has modeled them elsewhere; exclusion requires reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel technical analyses must be subject to notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Many aspects of the Final Rule’s futility analysis (sole reliance on particular metrics, three new de minimis thresholds, total vehicle emissions inventory, the 50% illustrative scenario, exclusive focus on CO2, and other quantitative assumptions and methodologies) were not in the proposal and thus represent new factual data, methods, and determinations to which commenters had no practicable opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under CAA §307(d)(7)(B) and administrative law, agencies may not rely on new technical analyses or key quantitative assumptions in a final rule if those analyses were not presented in the proposal and therefore were not subject to public comment; doing so requires mandatory reconsideration or supplemental notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of baseline year (2027) must be justified and non-circular
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA arbitrarily selected 2027 as the baseline year, thereby incorporating the reductions already achieved by past GHG standards into the baseline and using those baked-in benefits to argue the program is futile (circular reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses that purport to show futility of regulatory authority must consider appropriate baselines, including conditions at the time of the original endangerment finding and counterfactuals without prior regulations; agency must justify baseline choice and avoid circularly assuming away the effects of prior regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption that emissions flatline after 2055 requires support
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA arbitrarily assumed U.S. vehicle emissions will flatline after 2055 despite projections (MOVES, FHWA) showing continued increases in vehicle miles traveled (VMT) and no basis for believing VMT will stop growing or that fleet-performance improvements will offset increased travel absent regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model end-year and trend assumptions must be supported by evidence and aligned with authoritative projections; arbitrary truncation or implausible plateaus are legally infirm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of modeling endpoints (2050 and 2100) must capture long-term impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s focus on 2050 and 2100 as modeling endpoints significantly undervalues climate impacts because (1) the proportional contribution of U.S. vehicles is projected to grow over time (e.g., from ~4% to ~10% by 2100) and (2) GHGs persist for centuries, producing cumulative warming beyond 2100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must justify temporal endpoints and, where pollutants have long atmospheric lifetimes and cumulative effects, consider longer or more comprehensive time horizons (and demonstrate sensitivity to endpoint choices). Cherry-picking endpoints without explanation is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional-global-average metrics are an improper basis for de minimis/futility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated futility based on the proportional contribution of U.S. vehicle GHGs to global averages (global temperature and sea level) rather than the absolute or regional harms; this improperly treats small proportional shares as de minimis even when absolute impacts and local/regional harms are large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where harms may be catastrophic or geographically concentrated, even small proportional contributions can be legally and practically material; agencies must assess absolute, regional, and distributive impacts and cannot rely solely on relative global proportions to declare de minimis effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflation of statutory 'contribution' with 'measurability' and 'materiality' is unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA erred by conflating the Act’s requirement that emissions from a class of vehicles 'contribute' to dangerous air pollution with a prerequisite that regulation must have a 'measurable' or 'material' impact on those dangers before the Endangerment Finding or regulation is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory contribution is distinct from whether subsequent regulation will materially affect overall trends; agencies must apply the statute’s contribution standard and cannot add a judicially or administratively invented measurability/materiality precondition without reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an undefined or irrelevant 'climate measurability' comparative metric
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA arbitrarily selected an irrelevant comparative climate measurability metric (a 'scientific threshold for measurability') to compare alleged U.S. vehicle impacts to global trends—an approach commenters showed was legally and technically erroneous on numerous bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should select established, relevant metrics for comparative analysis (e.g., damage-based metrics, avoided harms) and explain why chosen measures are appropriate; selection of ad hoc or undefined thresholds without justification is arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to consider cumulative and long-term nature of GHG impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA ignored that GHG emissions are cumulative and long-lived—the warming effect of emissions persists for centuries and later emissions stack—so short or truncated modeling understates true harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses must account for atmospheric lifetimes and cumulative warming (and conduct sensitivity analyses over longer horizons) when assessing regulatory impacts for persistent pollutants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency with Agency precedent in assessing harms and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA acted inconsistently with its past practice in evaluating harms (e.g., historically considering damages and benefits rather than just proportional global metrics) and with how it has modeled other pollutants (ozone-depleting substances assessed over birth cohorts through 2100+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departures from longstanding agency practice require reasoned explanation; inconsistency without justification supports a finding of arbitrary and capricious action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular reasoning by 'baking in' prior regulatory benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: By using a baseline and assumptions that incorporate the technological and emissions reductions achieved by existing GHG standards, EPA effectively treats those regulatory successes as reasons the regulations are futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must avoid analytical circularity; when assessing whether regulation is futile, they should evaluate counterfactual scenarios that do not assume the regulatory effects they seek to invalidate, or otherwise explain why including prior regulatory effects is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model sensitivity and transparency obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s new modeling and quantitative assumptions are sensitive to differing assumptions and methodologies, yet the Agency failed to subject key elements to notice and comment or to provide adequate documentation and sensitivity analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical modeling underlying major policy conclusions must be transparent, reproducible, and accompanied by sensitivity/uncertainty analyses; agencies should disclose methods, data, and alternative scenarios to allow meaningful public comment and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to respond to and grapple with commenters’ criticisms (costs and other rationales)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA contradicted itself regarding whether costs informed its repeal of the vehicle GHG standards and failed to grapple with commenters’ criticisms of its proposed conclusions about costs; an agency must address significant comments and explain changes of position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must respond meaningfully to significant issues raised in comments (including cost analyses and objections to analytic approaches) and cannot ignore or superficially dismiss such criticisms when they are central to the final rule’s rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: New thresholds and arbitrary de minimis rules require reasoned explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Rule introduced three new de minimis thresholds and other threshold-based reasoning to support futility, but these thresholds were not justified in the proposal and appear arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds that determine whether regulatory authority exists or is exercised must be grounded in reasoned analysis, explained transparently, and exposed to public comment; introducing novel de minimis cutoffs without such treatment renders action arbitrary.
